record: Worried Germany might use the islands as a naval base, the US bought the Danish West Indies in 1917. They became the US Virgin Islands.

claim: A Japanese balloon bomb killed six people on a picnic in Oregon in 1945.
record: Japan launched thousands of hydrogen balloons carrying bombs on the jet stream toward North America. On 5 May 1945 one exploded near Bly, Oregon, killing a pregnant woman and five children.

claim: Some of the ashes of the man who designed the Pringles can were buried in a Pringles can.
record: Fredric Baur, the Procter & Gamble chemist who designed the stackable can, died in 2008. His family honoured his request and buried part of his ashes in one.

claim: Apple's third co-founder sold his 10 percent stake back for $800.
record: Ronald Wayne drew up Apple's partnership agreement with Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak and designed its first logo. Twelve days later he withdrew, fearing the financial risk.

claim: In 1698 Scotland tried to found its own colony in Panama.
record: The Darien scheme sank a large share of Scotland's available capital into a colony called New Caledonia. Disease, poor planning and Spanish opposition destroyed it, and the losses helped push Scotland toward union with England in 1707.

claim: The Pony Express mail service operated for only about 18 months.
record: Riders relayed mail between Missouri and California from April 1860 to October 1861. The transcontinental telegraph made it obsolete almost immediately.

claim: Gerald Ford became US president without ever being elected president or vice president.
record: Ford was appointed vice president under the 25th Amendment after Spiro Agnew resigned in 1973, then became president when Richard Nixon resigned in August 1974. He lost the 1976 election.

claim: British troops burned the White House during the War of 1812.
record: On 24 August 1814 British forces occupied Washington and set fire to the President's House, the Capitol and other buildings. First Lady Dolley Madison had the Gilbert Stuart portrait of Washington rescued first.

claim: In 1962 an outbreak of uncontrollable laughter forced schools to close in Tanganyika.
record: It began at a girls' boarding school in Kashasha and spread to villages over months, affecting around a thousand people. Researchers describe it as mass psychogenic illness.

claim: During Strasbourg's dancing plague of 1518, the city hired musicians to keep the dancers going.
record: Hundreds of people danced compulsively for weeks. Believing the dancers had to dance it out, the council opened guildhalls, built a stage and paid musicians, before changing course and sending sufferers to a shrine.

claim: Max Brod burned Franz Kafka's unpublished novels, as Kafka had instructed.
record: Kafka left written instructions for his friend to destroy his manuscripts unread. Brod refused and published 'The Trial', 'The Castle' and 'Amerika' after Kafka's death in 1924.

claim: American troops captured Quebec City on the last night of 1775.
record: Generals Richard Montgomery and Benedict Arnold attacked through a blizzard on 31 December 1775. Montgomery was killed, Arnold wounded, and hundreds of Americans captured.

claim: The House of Representatives impeached Richard Nixon in 1974.
record: The House Judiciary Committee approved three articles of impeachment in July 1974. Nixon resigned on 9 August before the full House could vote.

claim: President Nixon went on television in 1969 to mourn the Apollo 11 astronauts, stranded on the Moon.
record: Speechwriter William Safire wrote 'In Event of Moon Disaster' in case Armstrong and Aldrin could not lift off: 'Fate has ordained that the men who went to the Moon to explore in peace will stay on the Moon to rest in peace.' It was never needed.

claim: Guy Fawkes and his fellow plotters blew up the House of Lords in 1605.
record: Plotters packed 36 barrels of gunpowder into a cellar beneath the Lords, aiming to kill James I at the opening of Parliament. An anonymous warning letter led to a search, and Fawkes was arrested guarding the powder.

claim: A carpenter's time bomb killed Hitler in a Munich beer hall in 1939.
record: Georg Elser spent weeks hollowing out a pillar behind the speaker's podium. Hitler cut his speech short to catch a train and left 13 minutes before the bomb exploded, killing eight people.

claim: Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg's briefcase bomb killed Hitler in July 1944.
record: The bomb exploded at the Wolf's Lair on 20 July 1944, but the briefcase had been moved behind a heavy table leg. Hitler was only lightly injured, and the conspirators were hunted down.

claim: The Spanish Armada landed an invasion army in England in 1588.
record: The Armada was meant to escort the Duke of Parma's army across from Flanders. English fireships and attacks off Gravelines scattered it, and storms wrecked many ships on the way home.

claim: Australia voted to become a republic in 1999.
record: A referendum proposed replacing the Queen with a president chosen by Parliament. It was rejected by about 55 percent of voters and failed in every state.

claim: Gunmen assassinated French president Charles de Gaulle at Petit-Clamart in 1962.
record: Members of the OAS riddled de Gaulle's Citroën DS with bullets in August 1962. Two tyres were shot out, but the car kept going and no one inside was badly hurt.

claim: A Soviet submarine fired a nuclear torpedo at US warships during the Cuban Missile Crisis.
record: On 27 October 1962 US destroyers dropped signalling depth charges on submarine B-59. Crew accounts say the captain wanted to arm its nuclear torpedo; Vasili Arkhipov, whose agreement was reportedly needed, talked him down.

claim: In 1979 US bombers took off to retaliate after NORAD screens showed a massive Soviet missile attack.
record: On 9 November 1979 a training scenario was mistakenly fed into live warning systems. Fighters were scrambled and bomber crews alerted, but satellite and radar data showed no launch within minutes, and no retaliation was ordered.

claim: Captain FitzRoy refused to take Charles Darwin aboard the Beagle because of the shape of his nose.
record: Darwin later wrote that FitzRoy, a believer in physiognomy, doubted whether anyone with his nose could have enough energy for the voyage. FitzRoy took him anyway.

claim: Hubert Latham flew an aeroplane across the English Channel in July 1909.
record: Latham took off from near Calais on 19 July 1909, but his engine failed and he ditched in the sea, where he was found sitting on the floating plane. Louis Blériot made the first crossing six days later.

claim: Samuel Tilden, who won the popular vote in 1876, became president of the United States.
record: Tilden won the popular vote and was one electoral vote short of a majority when three states' results were disputed. A special commission awarded all of them to Rutherford B. Hayes.

claim: The first Great Seal of the United States, adopted in 1782, showed Moses parting the Red Sea.
record: In 1776 Franklin, Jefferson and Adams proposed a seal showing the Israelites crossing the Red Sea. Congress tabled it, and the 1782 design used the bald eagle instead.

sources.title: Great Seal of the United States

claim: Lincoln wrote the Gettysburg Address on the back of an envelope on the train.
record: Lincoln began drafting in Washington before he left and revised it in Gettysburg. The five known manuscript copies are on sheets of paper, not envelopes.
origin: The story appeared decades later and suited the image of Lincoln as an effortless genius.

claim: Thomas Edison personally electrocuted Topsy the elephant to show the dangers of his rival's AC power.
record: Topsy was killed at Coney Island's Luna Park in 1903 on the orders of the park's owners. There is no evidence Edison was involved, and the 'war of the currents' was long over.
origin: The execution was filmed by the Edison Manufacturing Company, and its name on the film fused the two stories.

claim: The 1918 'Spanish flu' pandemic started in Spain.
record: Where the pandemic began is still debated, with theories pointing to the United States, France and China. Spain was neutral in World War I, and its uncensored press reported the outbreak openly, so the name stuck.
origin: Wartime censors in the fighting nations suppressed flu news, so Spanish reports made it look like a Spanish disease.

claim: Cinco de Mayo celebrates Mexico's independence day.
record: Cinco de Mayo marks the Mexican army's victory over the French at the Battle of Puebla on 5 May 1862. Mexico's Independence Day is 16 September.
origin: The date became a big celebration of Mexican heritage in the United States, where many assume it marks independence.

claim: David Rice Atchison was president of the United States for one day in 1849.
record: Zachary Taylor's inauguration was delayed to Monday because 4 March fell on a Sunday. Taylor's term had legally begun anyway, and Atchison was never sworn in.
origin: Atchison's supporters later promoted the claim, and his gravestone calls him 'President of the United States for one day'.

claim: Betsy Ross designed the first American flag at George Washington's request.
record: Betsy Ross was a real Philadelphia upholsterer who made flags, but no contemporary record shows she designed or made the first Stars and Stripes.
origin: Her grandson William Canby told the story in a speech in 1870, nearly a century later, based on family tradition.

claim: The Liberty Bell cracked when it was rung to announce the Declaration of Independence.
record: No record shows the bell was rung for the Declaration in July 1776. The famous crack developed much later, most likely in the 1840s.
origin: An 1847 short story by George Lippard invented the scene of an old bellman ringing the bell for independence.

claim: Workers who died building the Hoover Dam are buried inside its concrete.
record: The dam was poured in relatively shallow blocks, so a fallen worker would have been found quickly. The Bureau of Reclamation says no one is entombed in it.
origin: The dam's scale, and the roughly one hundred deaths during construction, made the grim rumour easy to believe.

claim: The ancient Maya predicted the world would end in 2012.
record: The Maya Long Count calendar completed a major cycle, a b'ak'tun, in December 2012, much like an odometer rolling over. Maya inscriptions mention dates far beyond 2012.
origin: New Age writers from the 1970s onward turned the calendar date into a prophecy of doom or transformation.

claim: Roman gladiators routinely greeted the emperor with 'We who are about to die salute you.'
record: The phrase is recorded only once, by Suetonius, from a staged naval battle on the Fucine Lake in 52 CE, and those fighters were condemned prisoners, not gladiators.
origin: Nineteenth-century paintings, notably Jean-Léon Gérôme's, made it look like standard arena ritual.

claim: Columbus's crew feared they would sail off the edge of a flat Earth.
record: Educated Europeans had known the Earth was round since antiquity. The debate over Columbus was about its size: his critics correctly said Asia was much too far away.
origin: Washington Irving's romanticized 1828 biography of Columbus popularized the flat-Earth drama.

claim: Marie Antoinette responded to starving peasants with 'Let them eat cake.'
record: There is no evidence she said it. Jean-Jacques Rousseau attributed a similar line about brioche to 'a great princess' in his Confessions, written when Marie Antoinette was a child in Austria.
origin: Revolutionary pamphlets and later retellings pinned the arrogant remark on the unpopular queen.

claim: George Washington's false teeth were made of wood.
record: Washington's dentures were made from hippopotamus ivory, human teeth, animal teeth and metal springs. There is no evidence any were wooden.
origin: Stained, grainy ivory may have looked like wood, and the homespun image suited his legend.

claim: Galileo was thrown into a dungeon for saying the Earth goes around the Sun.
record: After his 1633 trial the Inquisition sentenced Galileo to imprisonment, but it was commuted to house arrest. He spent his last years at his villa in Arcetri and kept writing.
origin: Later retellings dramatized his punishment, turning house arrest into a dungeon.

claim: The US Senate ratified the Treaty of Versailles and took America into the League of Nations.
record: President Wilson championed the League, but the Senate rejected the treaty in November 1919 and again in March 1920, when it fell seven votes short of the two-thirds needed. The US never joined.

claim: Allied troops invaded Japan's home islands in November 1945.
record: Operation Downfall planned landings on Kyushu for November 1945 and near Tokyo in 1946, the largest amphibious assault ever prepared. Japan announced its surrender in August, and the invasion was cancelled.

claim: Retreating German forces blew up Paris's bridges and landmarks in August 1944, as Hitler had ordered.
record: Hitler ordered that Paris should fall into Allied hands only as a field of ruins, and explosives were laid under bridges. The garrison commander, Dietrich von Choltitz, surrendered the city largely intact on 25 August.

claim: The United States bought Cuba from Spain in 1848.
record: President James K. Polk authorised an offer of $100 million for Cuba in 1848. Spain refused, and later American attempts to buy or seize the island also failed.

claim: Charles Babbage completed his Difference Engine for the British government in the 1830s.
record: The government put about £17,000 into Babbage's calculating machine, but only a small working section was assembled. The project was abandoned in 1842; a full engine was finally built from his plans by the Science Museum in 1991.

claim: An Arab army captured Constantinople in 718.
record: The Umayyad Caliphate besieged the Byzantine capital by land and sea for about a year. Greek fire, a harsh winter, famine and Bulgarian attacks forced the survivors to retreat in 718.

claim: Napoleon's army crossed the English Channel and invaded Britain in 1805.
record: Napoleon massed around 200,000 men and a flotilla of invasion barges at Boulogne. Without control of the Channel he turned the army east against Austria in August 1805, and Trafalgar ended the threat that October.

sources.title: Napoleon%27s planned invasion of the United Kingdom

claim: Bonnie Prince Charlie's Jacobite army captured London in 1745.
record: The Jacobites marched from Scotland as far as Derby, about 125 miles from London, where news of their advance caused panic. On 6 December 1745 their commanders voted to turn back north.

claim: Britain went to war with the US in 1861 after Americans seized two Confederate envoys from a British ship.
record: A US warship stopped the British mail steamer Trent and removed Confederate diplomats. Britain sent thousands of troops to Canada and demanded an apology; Lincoln's government released the men, and war was avoided.

claim: Samuel Langley's piloted Aerodrome flew over the Potomac in 1903, days before the Wright brothers.
record: Backed by War Department money, Langley's machine was catapulted from a houseboat twice in 1903. Both times it plunged into the Potomac; the second crash came on 8 December, nine days before the Wrights flew at Kitty Hawk.

claim: In 1958 Martin Luther King Jr. was stabbed in the chest at a Harlem book signing and survived.
record: Izola Ware Curry stabbed King with a letter opener that came to rest next to his aorta. Surgeons later told him that if he had sneezed he could have died.

claim: Emperor Nero played the fiddle while Rome burned in 64 CE.
record: The fiddle had not been invented. Tacitus says Nero was at Antium when the fire broke out and rushed back to organise relief; the rumour at the time was that he sang about the fall of Troy.
origin: Hostile ancient writers such as Suetonius and Cassius Dio reported the singing, and English retellings turned his lyre into a fiddle.

claim: The Pilgrims stepped ashore onto Plymouth Rock in 1620.
record: No account written by the Pilgrims mentions a rock. The boulder was identified in 1741, more than 120 years later, by a 94-year-old man recalling what he had been told as a boy.
origin: Thomas Faunce's 1741 identification turned an ordinary boulder into a national relic.

claim: Thomas Crapper invented the flush toilet.
record: Sir John Harington designed a flushing toilet in the 1590s, and Alexander Cumming patented the S-bend in 1775. Crapper was a Victorian plumber who ran a successful business and patented improvements such as the ballcock.
origin: A 1969 comic biography, 'Flushed with Pride', exaggerated his inventions, and his name on cisterns did the rest.

claim: The Great Chicago Fire of 1871 was started by Mrs O'Leary's cow kicking over a lantern.
record: The fire did start near the O'Leary barn, but no one proved how. In 1893 reporter Michael Ahern admitted he had invented the cow story, and the city council cleared Catherine O'Leary in 1997.
origin: A reporter's colourful story played on prejudice against Irish immigrants and outlived every official finding.

claim: Albert Einstein worked on the Manhattan Project to build the first atomic bomb.
record: Einstein signed the 1939 letter warning President Roosevelt that Germany might build a bomb, but he was denied a security clearance and did not work on the Manhattan Project.
origin: His famous equation and his signature on the letter tied his name to the bomb in public memory.

claim: The Titanic sent the first SOS distress call in history.
record: SOS was adopted as an international distress signal in 1906 and came into use from 1908, and ships used it before 1912. The Titanic's operators sent both the older CQD and SOS.
origin: The disaster's fame made the Titanic's SOS the one everyone remembered.

claim: Napoleon's soldiers shot the nose off the Great Sphinx.
record: Drawings made decades before Napoleon's 1798 campaign already show the Sphinx without its nose. The 15th-century historian al-Maqrizi reported that a Sufi zealot damaged the face in 1378.
origin: Napoleon's famous Egyptian expedition made his troops convenient culprits.

claim: As a boy, George Washington chopped down his father's cherry tree and confessed: 'I cannot tell a lie.'
record: No evidence supports the tale. It first appeared in the fifth edition of Mason Locke Weems's biography of Washington, published in 1806, years after Washington's death.
origin: Parson Weems wrote moralizing, invented anecdotes to make Washington a model for children.

claim: Each Scottish clan has worn its own tartan pattern since ancient times.
record: Before the 18th century tartans varied by region and weaver rather than clan. Most 'clan tartans' were named and standardized in the 19th century, helped by the forged 1842 book 'Vestiarium Scoticum'.
origin: George IV's 1822 visit to Edinburgh set off a Highland craze, and manufacturers happily assigned patterns to clans.

claim: Saint Patrick drove the snakes out of Ireland.
record: There is no evidence Ireland had native snakes after the last Ice Age; they never recolonized the island once it was cut off by the sea.
origin: The story, first recorded centuries after Patrick's death, is usually read as a metaphor for his driving out paganism.

claim: Friday the 13th became unlucky because the Knights Templar were arrested on that day in 1307.
record: The Templars were arrested in France on Friday, 13 October 1307, but no record links the date to bad luck until the 20th century. Fear of Friday the 13th as such appears in writing only from the 19th century.
origin: Novels, most famously 'The Da Vinci Code', popularized the Templar connection.
